body: Wanting things done well is a good quality. Over the next ninety days, you get to find out where it helps you and where it quietly wears you down.
Perfectionism often looks like high standards from the outside. From the inside, it can feel more like never being allowed to rest.
Today, just notice the moments you redo something that was already fine. No need to change anything yet.
Most perfectionism began as a way to feel safe or approved of. It made sense back then. You can thank it and still loosen its grip.
Pay attention to the phrase "it's not ready yet." Count how many times it shows up in your thinking today.
There is a difference between caring about quality and being afraid of criticism. They can feel identical until you look closely.
Notice where you spend the last twenty percent of effort. Sometimes it matters. Often nobody else would ever see it.
You might be tired in a particular way: the tiredness of checking, rechecking and polishing. That tiredness is worth taking seriously.
Perfectionism can make you start late, because starting means risking a less than perfect result. Today, simply notice if that is you.
Write down one area where your standards feel heavy. Just name it. Naming it is the first loosening.
Ask yourself who you are trying to satisfy with this level of polish. Sometimes the answer is a person who is no longer in your life.
A mistake is information, not a verdict on who you are.
Notice how your body feels when you hand something in. Tight shoulders and a held breath are clues worth paying attention to.
You can hold high standards and still be kind to the person meeting them. That person is you.
Look at something you made a year ago that you thought was not good enough. Does it still look as bad as it felt then?
"Good enough" is not the same as careless. It means the work does its job and you get to keep some energy for your life.
Today, notice the gap between what was asked of you and what you are asking of yourself.
Perfectionism tends to hide in small places: the email reread five times, the message deleted and retyped. Look for it there.
You do not have to fix this. For now, getting curious about it is plenty.
Imagine the people who love you seeing your work. Would they want you to suffer this much over it?
Try a tiny experiment today: send one message after reading it once, not three times.
Notice what happens after you let something go out imperfect. Usually, much less than you feared.
Choose one low-stakes task and give it a time limit. When the timer ends, it is done.
A finished thing that is decent helps more people than a perfect thing that never leaves your desk.
Try asking "What would seventy percent look like here?" Then see if seventy percent is actually enough.
Today, leave one small thing slightly undone. A drawer not quite tidy, a list not quite complete. Notice how long the discomfort lasts.
The urge to keep tweaking often rises and falls like a wave. If you wait it out, it usually passes.
When the inner voice says "not good enough," try asking "good enough for what?" The answer is often smaller than you thought.
Share a draft with someone before it feels finished. Early feedback is usually kinder than the judge in your head.
Perfectionism counts what is missing. Today, try counting what is already there.
Notice whether you celebrate finishing things or just move straight to the next worry. A small pause to mark it matters.
Pick one area of life where good enough is truly fine: laundry, a quick lunch, a reply to a group chat. Practise there first.
You can redo less and live more. Both are skills, and both improve with use.
If you procrastinate on something, ask whether perfectionism is underneath. Lowering the bar can make starting possible.
Try writing a deliberately rough first version of something today. Call it a sketch. Sketches are allowed to be messy.
Other people's mistakes probably do not make you think less of them. Try offering yourself the same easy forgiveness.
Today, ask someone you trust how they decide when something is finished. Their answer may surprise you.
Notice the difference between "this could be better" and "this needs to be better." Only one of them is true most of the time.
When you catch yourself polishing, gently ask: is this for the work, or for my nerves?
Perfectionism can make rest feel earned rather than given. You are allowed to rest before everything is done.
Try a small imperfect thing on purpose: wear the slightly creased shirt, send the email with a typo you noticed after.
Doing something badly for the first time is how everyone begins. Beginners are not supposed to be polished.
If you feel anxious after letting something go, that is not proof you made a mistake. It is just the old habit protesting.
Today, set a "done" line before you start a task. Decide in advance what finished looks like.
Speed and care can live together. A quick, thoughtful job is still a thoughtful job.
Notice how often you compare your behind-the-scenes to someone else's highlights. Their work had drafts too.
Your worth was never meant to rest on the quality of your output. You were enough before you made anything.
Practise accepting a compliment today without adding a "but." Just say thank you.
Look back at the experiments so far. Which ones felt hardest? Which ones turned out easier than you expected?
Halfway in. If you have caught yourself even a few times, the habit is already less automatic than it was.
Try saying "that's done" out loud when you finish something. Words can help your mind accept an ending.
Notice the freedom in a decision you did not overthink. There is often more of it than you expect.
Some things deserve your very best effort. Saving it for them is wiser than spending it on everything.
Pick one thing this week that matters most. Let the others be good enough so that one can be great.
Imperfect action builds confidence faster than perfect planning.
When you make a mistake today, try responding like a calm coach: "Okay, what's next?"
Letting things be good enough frees up time. Notice what you choose to do with that time.
You might find people relate to you more when you are a little less polished. Imperfection is easy to warm to.
The goal is not to stop caring. It is to care in a way that leaves something left over for you.
Try a hobby where you are not good yet. Being bad at something on purpose is excellent practice.
Notice whether your standards for yourself are higher than your standards for anyone else. Fairness can apply to you too.
Today, deliberately stop one task five minutes early. See whether anything is actually lost.
You are learning to trust that good enough really is enough. That trust grows each time you test it and nothing breaks.
Ask yourself what you would attempt if you knew it did not have to be perfect.
Some of your best moments probably came from things that went off script. Leave room for that.
You are becoming someone who finishes things and moves on. That is a quiet kind of strength.
When the old voice returns, you do not need to argue. "I hear you, and I'm going with this version" is enough.
Notice how much lighter your days feel when you are not carrying every small decision around afterwards.
Try finishing a task and not checking it again. Trust the version of you who did it.
People rarely remember the flaw you fretted over. They remember whether you showed up.
Relaxing your standards in small places is a skill, not a lowering of who you are.
You can like your work and still see how it could be better next time. Both thoughts are allowed at once.
Today, notice one thing you let be imperfect this week that turned out completely fine.
You do not need to earn a slower pace. Moving gently is a choice you are allowed to make.
Consider writing yourself a short permission note: "I am allowed to hand things in that are good enough."
The new habits may wobble when you are stressed. That is normal. Return to them without making it a big deal.
More finished things, fewer abandoned perfect plans. That is what this change can look like in practice.
Notice how you talk about your work now compared to a couple of months ago. Small shifts in language matter.
You have started choosing where to put your best effort instead of spending it everywhere. That is real growth.
Perfection was always moving further away. Good enough is somewhere you can actually arrive.
Someone else may be watching how you handle mistakes and learning from you. Your gentleness can give them permission too.
Today, do one thing simply because you enjoy it, with no aim to do it well.
You are learning that a mistake can be small. It does not have to grow into a story about who you are.
Look back at the first week of this. What did you believe then that you no longer quite believe now?
Name three things you finished recently that were good enough. Let yourself be pleased with them.
Some days the old perfectionism will feel strong. That does not erase the progress. It just means you are human.
Your high standards are still yours. You are simply the one deciding when to use them now.
Keep one experiment from these weeks as a regular habit. Pick the one that gave you the most relief.
Ninety days ago, good enough may have felt like failure. Notice what it feels like now.
When you notice the pull to perfect something, take one breath and ask whether this moment really calls for it.
You can carry this forward: care deeply, finish kindly, and let things go out into the world.
Good enough has been good to you. Keep letting it be.
